sentences.text: This small shark grew to a length between 15 and 50 centimeters.
Its teeth possessed a single central point, a base that widened toward the tongue side, and many blood-filled channels.
Remains of this animal have been found in both salty and fresh waters across the globe.
Fossils show it likely lived on the bottom of the ocean and crushed hard shells for food.
The genus was first named by Brough in 1935.
Complete skulls and body parts from the Early Triassic species L. cassangensis and L. africanus were discovered in Angola and South Africa.
Lissodus is an extinct member of the hybodont sharks.
Its parent group is the Hybodontiformes.
The animal belongs to the class Chondrichthyes.
It is usually placed in the family Lonchidiidae, though some experts consider its position uncertain within Hybodontiformes.
Fossils appear from the latest Devonian to the end of the Cretaceous, although some researchers believe the range is narrower, extending only from the Early Triassic to the Early Cretaceous.
The species lived from the Tournaisian to the Campanian, a span from 358.86 to 72.2 million years ago.
Some scientists question whether Lissodus is a valid genus, proposing that its unique teeth are simply a juvenile trait found in many hybodonts.
